student_authored_expectations.source_performance: Stronger MMD will probably hurt source performance while making the source domains look more similar to each other. Here is why. MMD adds a penalty that tries to force the average features from different domains to match. So if you turn up the MMD weight, the model starts caring more about making domains indistinguishable and less about the actual classification job. As that pressure grows, the features get squeezed into a shared space, and some of the information that helped tell source classes apart can get lost. That means source validation accuracy and macro F1 will likely drop, at least a little. At the same time, the score that measures how well you can tell the source domains apart should go down and get closer to chance, since that is exactly what MMD is trying to do. The effect on the target or unseen domain is the tricky part. A little alignment might help by removing domain specific noise, but too much can backfire and cause negative transfer, where useful class information gets erased. So the relationship is probably not a straight line. Some alignment helps, but too much hurts. The reason is that the two losses are pulling in different directions. Cross entropy wants features that separate classes, while MMD wants features that look the same no matter the domain. When the MMD weight gets large, it takes over, and the model may satisfy it by making features too similar and blurring class boundaries. So in short, stronger MMD likely means lower source accuracy and F1, lower domain separability, and possibly worse target performance if class information is lost.
student_authored_expectations.domain_separability: Stronger MMD should make domain separability go down. That is basically the whole point of MMD. It pushes the average features from different domains to match, so a classifier trying to tell which domain an example came from will have a harder time. If the alignment is strong, that score should drop toward chance, which is about 33 percent when you have three source domains. But there is a catch. Lower separability does not automatically mean the model got better. It could also mean the features got squashed together and lost useful class information along the way. So yes, stronger MMD likely lowers domain separability, but you still need to check whether source and target performance hold up, because a low separability score on its own does not prove the alignment helped.
student_authored_expectations.sketch_recognition: Stronger MMD could help Sketch recognition, but only up to a point. The idea is that if the model learns features that look the same across Photo, Art Painting, and Cartoon, those features might also carry over better to Sketch, which is a very different visual domain. So a bit of alignment could close the domain gap and give you a small boost on Sketch. But if you push the MMD weight too high, the features get squashed together too much, and the model starts losing the class information it needs to tell a dog from a cat or a horse from a cow. When that happens, Sketch recognition can actually get worse than the plain ERM baseline. This is negative transfer. So the likely pattern is a curve that goes up and then down. A little MMD helps, a lot hurts. And you cannot really know where the sweet spot is without running the experiment, because it depends on how much class information gets erased along the way.
